Its open, fifth-dominated sound evokes windswept coastal landscapes and became a primary influence on American folk, country, and bluegrass music through Irish and Scottish emigration.
scales.usage: Irish traditional music, Scottish folk, uilleann pipes, fiddle tunes, sean-nós singing, bluegrass.
scales.characteristicPatterns: Ornamental cuts and rolls between the b3 and 4 are idiomatic. Slow descending phrases from the 5th. Drone on root and fifth.

rhythmPatterns.name: Jig
rhythmPatterns.description: Fundamental Celtic dance rhythm in compound duple time

rhythmPatterns.name: Reel
rhythmPatterns.description: Fast Celtic dance in cut time, driving eighth-note feel

rhythmPatterns.name: Slow Air
rhythmPatterns.description: Unmeasured, deeply ornamented expression of slow Irish airs

songExamples.title: Irish Slow Air Celtic Minor Pentatonic Fiddle

scales.name: Flamenco Scale
scales.description:
The Flamenco scale (also called Phrygian dominant or Frigio Mayor) is the defining tonal element of flamenco music — a fusion of Romani, Moorish, Jewish, and Castilian musical traditions that developed in Andalusia, Spain. It is identical to the fifth mode of harmonic minor but carries its own distinct ornamental vocabulary.

In flamenco, this scale is not merely a note collection but a system of melodic gestures: the characteristic Andalusian cadence (bVII-bVI-V-i), the falseta (melodic interlude), and the picado (rapid scalar runs) are all rooted in this scale. Each flamenco palo (form) — soleares, seguiriyas, bulerías, alegrías — employs the scale with distinct rhythmic and emotional character.
scales.usage: Flamenco guitar, cante jondo (deep song), flamenco dance accompaniment, Spanish classical guitar.
scales.characteristicPatterns: The Andalusian cadence (descending from bVII to I). Rapid ascending runs. Heavy use of the b2 as an expressive tone. Rasgueado strumming patterns.

rhythmPatterns.name: Bulería
rhythmPatterns.description: Fastest flamenco compás, complex accents, highly syncopated

rhythmPatterns.name: Soleá
rhythmPatterns.description: The mother of all flamenco forms, stately and deep

rhythmPatterns.name: Seguiriya
rhythmPatterns.description: The deepest, most anguished flamenco form

scales.name: Chahargah
scales.description:
Chahargah (meaning 'fourth place' or 'fourth position') is one of the twelve main dastgahs of Persian classical music. It has a powerful, heroic character with a characteristic augmented second in its lower tetrachord that immediately sets it apart from the other dastgahs.

In Persian music, a dastgah is more than a scale — it is an entire melodic system with prescribed phrases, modulations, and emotional associations. Chahargah is associated with power and heroism, and is frequently used in epic contexts. It shares interval structure with the Turkish Nikriz makam, reflecting centuries of musical exchange between Persian and Ottoman cultures.
scales.usage: Persian classical music (radif), tar and setar solos, traditional Persian ensemble, sacred and ceremonial music.
scales.characteristicPatterns: Characteristic ascending phrase emphasizing the augmented second. The #4 (Chahargah's defining note) is approached with specific ornamentation called tahrir.

rhythmPatterns.name: Chahargah Avaz
rhythmPatterns.description: Unmeasured improvisation (avaz) in the Chahargah dastgah

rhythmPatterns.name: Chahargah Reng
rhythmPatterns.description: Measured dance-like section within Chahargah performance

scales.name: Vietnamese Pentatonic
scales.description:
Vietnamese traditional music uses a variety of pentatonic modes, with the southern Vietnamese pentatonic (thang am nam) being perhaps the most characteristic. It differs from Chinese and other East Asian pentatonics through its use of microtonal ornaments — bends, slides, and vibrato techniques that cannot be captured in standard notation.

This scale underlies traditional forms including Nhã nhạc (royal court music, UNESCO heritage), Đờn ca tài tử (southern amateur music), and Cải lương (reformed opera). The đàn tranh (16-string zither), đàn bầu (monochord), and đàn nguyệt (moon lute) are the primary vehicles for this scale.
scales.usage: Vietnamese court music, Đờn ca tài tử, Cải lương opera, đàn tranh and đàn bầu solos.
scales.characteristicPatterns: Characteristic microtonal bends particularly on the b3 and 6. Ornamented descending phrases. Drone on root.

rhythmPatterns.name: Nam Ai
rhythmPatterns.description: Slow, expressive unmeasured form associated with deep emotion

rhythmPatterns.name: Ly Con Sao
rhythmPatterns.description: Moderate folk song rhythm from central Vietnam

songExamples.title: Nha Nhac Vietnamese Court Music UNESCO

scales.name: Gnawa Scale
scales.description:
The Gnawa musical tradition of Morocco descends from Sub-Saharan African slaves brought to North Africa centuries ago, blending Islamic mysticism with pre-Islamic animist ritual. Gnawa music is inseparable from the lila — an all-night healing ceremony in which musicians invoke spiritual entities (mluk) through specific melodic colors, each associated with a different spirit, color, and emotional state.

The scale played on the guembri (three-string bass lute) has a deep, hypnotic quality. The music influenced 1960s rock psychedelia (Jimi Hendrix recorded in Morocco), and Gnawa fusion has become an important genre in contemporary world music.
scales.usage: Lila healing ceremonies, Sufi-influenced spiritual music, world music fusion, contemporary Moroccan music.
scales.characteristicPatterns: Heavy repetitive bass lines on guembri. Cascading metal qraqeb (castanets) in syncopated patterns. Trance-inducing cyclical phrases.

rhythmPatterns.name: Gnawa Lila
rhythmPatterns.description: Hypnotic repeated cycle with syncopated qraqeb (castanets)

rhythmPatterns.name: Maalem Pattern
rhythmPatterns.description: Driving 6/8 feel for energetic Gnawa sections

scales.name: Scottish Mixolydian
scales.description:
Scottish folk music has a strong Mixolydian character, using the natural seventh (b7) rather than the leading tone. This gives Scottish melodies their characteristic sense of unresolved forward motion — powerful yet never quite landing, suggesting something beyond the horizon.

The Highland bagpipe (great Highland pipes) is inherently Mixolydian because of its fixed tuning and lack of a standard leading tone. Countless Scottish reels, strathspeys, marches, and laments use this mode. It also flows into Irish traditional music through shared cultural history.
scales.usage: Scottish folk music, Highland pipe tunes, strathspeys, reels, marches, laments.
scales.characteristicPatterns: Characteristic movement between the 6th and b7th degrees. Strong melodic phrases ending on the 5th or root without strong leading-tone resolution.

rhythmPatterns.name: Strathspey
rhythmPatterns.description: Scottish dance with characteristic 'Scotch snap' (short-long) rhythm

rhythmPatterns.name: March
rhythmPatterns.description: Military and ceremonial pipe march feel

rhythmPatterns.name: Slow Strathspey
rhythmPatterns.description: Stately version of the strathspey for airs and laments

scales.name: Segah
scales.description:
Segah (meaning 'third place') is one of the twelve dastgahs of Persian classical music and one of the most intimate and spiritual. It uses characteristic microtonal intervals — particularly a slightly lowered third degree — that cannot be reproduced on equal-tempered instruments.

Segah is deeply associated with the Islamic call to prayer and devotional contexts. The famous Persian musician Shajarian has performed some of his most celebrated recordings in Segah. The dastgah has a warm, inward quality very different from the heroic Chahargah or the melancholic Shur.
scales.usage: Persian classical radif, devotional and spiritual contexts, tar and setar, vocal improvisation.
scales.characteristicPatterns: The lowered third (koron) is the defining feature. Characteristic gusheh (melodic module) phrases circle around the b3 and resolve to the root.

rhythmPatterns.name: Segah Avaz
rhythmPatterns.description: Unmeasured vocal or instrumental improvisation in Segah

rhythmPatterns.name: Tasnif
rhythmPatterns.description: Measured song form in the Persian classical tradition

scales.name: Okinawan Scale
scales.description:
The Okinawan (Ryukyuan) pentatonic scale is strikingly distinct from both mainland Japanese and Chinese scales, reflecting Okinawa's unique position as a trading crossroads between Japan, China, and Southeast Asia. Its defining feature is the coexistence of a minor third and a natural (major) third — a neutral quality found in almost no other scale tradition.

The scale is played primarily on the sanshin (Okinawan three-string lute, ancestor of the Japanese shamisen) and is at the core of traditional Ryukyuan music including kachāshī (celebratory dance), narrative songs, and court music. The 2024 Oscar-winning song 'Naatu Naatu' and the global resurgence of Okinawan music have brought renewed attention to this distinctive sound.
scales.usage: Okinawan sanshin music, Ryukyuan court music, kachāshī dance, contemporary J-pop with Okinawan flavor.
scales.characteristicPatterns: The major third following the minor third is the key gesture. Bright, celebratory upward phrases. Often played with a cheerful rhythmic feel.

rhythmPatterns.name: Kachāshī
rhythmPatterns.description: Lively Okinawan celebratory dance rhythm, fast and joyful

rhythmPatterns.name: Yotsudake
rhythmPatterns.description: Okinawan castanet-accompanied rhythmic pattern

scales.name: Mongolian Pentatonic
scales.description:
The Mongolian pentatonic scale underlies the vast repertoire of Mongolian traditional music, from the sweeping urtiin duu (long songs) of the steppes to the rapid, rhythmic bogino duu (short songs). While the interval structure resembles the Chinese Gong mode and Western major pentatonic, Mongolian music gives it a distinctive character through vast open melodic leaps, glottal ornaments, and the overtone-rich timbre of the morin khuur (horsehead fiddle) and tovshuur (lute).

Mongolian urtiin duu — UNESCO-recognized intangible cultural heritage — features extraordinarily long vocal phrases with minimal accompaniment, evoking the infinite landscape of the Mongolian steppe. Khoomei (throat singing), in which singers simultaneously produce a drone and a high whistle tone, often elaborates the overtone series of this scale.
scales.usage: Urtiin duu (long song), bogino duu (short song), khoomei performance, morin khuur solos, Mongolian court and folk music.
scales.characteristicPatterns: Wide leaping intervals across multiple octaves. Extremely long phrases with minimal breath. The pentatonic avoids semitones, giving open spacious quality.

rhythmPatterns.name: Urtiin Duu
rhythmPatterns.description: Unmeasured, freely flowing long-phrase vocal style with vast range

rhythmPatterns.name: Bogino Duu
rhythmPatterns.description: Measured short-song rhythm, quicker and more dance-oriented

scales.name: Tibetan Folk Scale
scales.description:
Tibetan traditional music spans sacred Buddhist ceremony and secular folk, with a pentatonic framework underlying much of the folk repertoire. The dramnyen (six-string lute) and lingbu (transverse flute) are the primary melodic instruments of Tibetan folk music, while sacred music uses dungchen (long trumpets), dung dkar (conch shells), and rolmo (cymbals) that create washes of sound rather than melody.

Tibetan folk songs (lo-gzhas) and dance songs (gzhas-gzhas) use this pentatonic framework with a characteristic style of ornamentation and microtonal inflection that reflects the thin-air acoustics of high altitude living. Tibetan music is also heavily influenced by its role in Buddhist meditation practice, where sustained tones and harmonics induce contemplative states.
scales.usage: Tibetan folk songs, lo-gzhas (folk songs), dramnyen lute music, informal community music.
scales.characteristicPatterns: Simple repeated pentatonic phrases. Upward melodic movement from the 4th to 5th is characteristic. Drone on the root.

rhythmPatterns.name: Gzhas
rhythmPatterns.description: Standard folk dance song rhythm from Tibet

rhythmPatterns.name: Free Ceremonial
rhythmPatterns.description: Unmeasured sacred/ceremonial Tibetan Buddhist music context

scales.name: Rittsu Mode
scales.description:
The Rittsu mode (ritsu-chō) is one of the two foundational pentatonic modes in Japanese court music (gagaku), the other being the brighter Ryō mode. Imported from Tang dynasty China along with gagaku itself in the 7th–8th centuries, Rittsu corresponds to the Chinese Lü scale and is built on a minor-flavored pentatonic with a lowered seventh.

In Japanese gagaku, Rittsu melodies are traditionally assigned to the autumn and winter seasons and are associated with introspection and solemnity. The mode is played on the shō (mouth organ), hichiriki (double-reed pipe), and ryūteki (transverse flute). Contemporary Japanese composers and musicians continue to draw on Rittsu mode for its distinctive, grounded character.
scales.usage: Japanese gagaku court music, Buddhist ceremonial music, contemporary Japanese composition.
scales.characteristicPatterns: Smooth pentatonic movement emphasizing the lowered seventh. Sustained tones on the shō create harmonic clusters around the mode's notes.

rhythmPatterns.name: Gagaku Free Meter
rhythmPatterns.description: Gagaku uses extremely slow, unmeasured pacing guided by drum signals

rhythmPatterns.name: Etenraku
rhythmPatterns.description: The most famous gagaku piece, in measured moderate tempo

scales.name: Raga Kafi
scales.description:
Raga Kafi belongs to the Kafi thaat (parent scale) and is classified as a late-night raga traditionally performed between 9 pm and midnight. Its Dorian-like character — with a flat third and flat seventh but natural second and sixth — gives it a romantic, slightly wistful quality distinct from the heavier evening ragas.

Kafi is associated with the spring season (Vasant) and is one of the oldest ragas in the Hindustani system, with roots in dhrupad performance. It has spawned an entire family of derivative ragas including Bageshri, Sindhura, and Pilu.
scales.usage: Classical Khyal and Dhrupad performances, light-classical thumri and dadra, folk songs of the Gangetic plains, and devotional music.
scales.characteristicPatterns: Andolita (oscillating) notes on the Ga and Ni; characteristic ascending phrases that skip from Sa to Pa; descending lines that linger on Ga and Ni.

rhythmPatterns.name: Teentaal
rhythmPatterns.description: Medium Teentaal (16 beats, 4×4) — Raga Kafi is presented across all tempos, but medium Teentaal is the most common format for Khyal performances.

rhythmPatterns.name: Keherwa
rhythmPatterns.description: Keherwa (8 beats) — a light, popular tala used for thumri and dadra in Kafi, reflecting the raga's connection to folk and semi-classical traditions.

scales.name: Ethiopian Ambassel
scales.description:
The Ambassel mode is one of the principal scales of Ethiopian music, used in the highlands of the Amhara and Tigrinya peoples. Its major-pentatonic character — built on whole steps and minor thirds — gives it a luminous, open quality associated with religious praise, festivity, and the bright morning hours.

Ambasselse music is closely tied to the begena (a large 10-string lyre regarded as sacred) and the masenqo (single-string bowed lute). Its symmetrical interval structure — alternating whole tones and minor thirds — makes it particularly suited to the call-and-response singing style of Ethiopian folk and sacred music.
scales.usage: Ethiopian Orthodox Christian sacred music, Amhara wedding songs, festive and ceremonial occasions, begena lyre music.
scales.characteristicPatterns: Call-and-response between soloist and chorus; pentatonic melodic sequences in 6/8 feel; melismatic ornamentation of scale degrees 2 and 4.

rhythmPatterns.name: Eskista 6/8
rhythmPatterns.description: Compound 6/8 groove underlying Eskista shoulder dancing — the rolling compound meter captures the buoyant, dance-ready character of Ambassel celebrations.

rhythmPatterns.name: Begena free meter
rhythmPatterns.description: Free-meter begena improvisation — in sacred contexts the scale is played without strict rhythm, with long resonant tones on the lyre creating a meditative, hypnotic atmosphere.

scales.name: Yoruba Pentatonic
scales.description:
The Yoruba pentatonic scale is central to the music of the Yoruba people of southwestern Nigeria and Benin, one of Africa's most musically influential cultures. It forms the melodic foundation for jùjú music, fúji, and much traditional music associated with the Yoruba Ọrìṣà (deity) worship system.

This scale's characteristic interval pattern — two whole steps, a minor third, two more whole steps, and a closing minor third — generates melodies of great warmth and forward momentum. It underpins the polyrhythmic talking-drum music (dùndún) that 'speaks' the tonal Yoruba language, as well as the sacred songs (oríkì) used in Ọrìṣà ceremonies.
scales.usage: Jùjú music, fúji, traditional Ọrìṣà ceremonies, talking-drum compositions, contemporary Afrobeats melodic foundations.
scales.characteristicPatterns: Cyclical melodic ostinatos over polyrhythmic percussion; call-and-response between soloist and chorus; talking-drum melodic imitation; pentatonic runs in 12/8.

rhythmPatterns.name: Dùndún 12/8
rhythmPatterns.description: Yoruba dùndún talking-drum groove in 12/8 — the compound triple feel allows the melodic pentatonic scale to be 'spoken' through tonal percussion in the 3-against-2 West African polyrhythmic framework.

rhythmPatterns.name: Jùjú 4/4
rhythmPatterns.description: Jùjú groove — the modern Yoruba popular style pioneered by King Sunny Ade, combining the pentatonic scale with steel-guitar, talking-drum, and syncopated 4/4.
